documents.title: CUNY Academic Integrity Policy (2024)
documents.summary: System-wide CUNY academic integrity policy revised in 2024 to add AI. It writes AI into the definitions of cheating and plagiarism, requires citation of AI content, defers permitted use to each syllabus or instructor, and sets reporting, sanction and hearing procedures plus a rationale for teaching responsible AI use.
documents.stance_why: The policy sets no AI rule of its own beyond classing unauthorized AI use as cheating and plagiarism; it states that 'Any use of generative AI tools must be in line with the usage policy for specific assignments as defined in the course of the syllabus and/or communicated by the course instructor', which hands the decision to instructors.

units.why: The CUNY policy defines cheating to include 'artificial intelligence (AI) systems' used without authorization, so unauthorized AI use is classed as misconduct; this is the misconduct-classification type (P36), not a ban on a specific output.
units.anchor: devices, artificial intelligence (AI) systems, or communication during an academic exercise
units.frag_start: is the unauthorized use or attempted
units.policy: Unauthorized use or attempted use of artificial intelligence (AI) systems during an academic exercise is cheating.

units.why: Listing 'Copying ... from a generative AI system' as an example of cheating bars students from copying AI output into work submitted for credit; P19 (AI may not produce submitted work) fits better than P36 because the rule names the prohibited act.
units.anchor: Copying from another person or from a generative AI system
units.policy: Copying from a generative AI system, or allowing others to copy work submitted for credit or a grade, is cheating.

units.why: The sentence 'Any use of generative AI tools must be in line with the usage policy for specific assignments' hands the permission decision to each course or assignment, which is P04 (instructor or assignment sets the rule); it sets no university-wide default.
units.anchor: generative AI tools must be in line with the usage policy for specific assignments
units.frag_start: Any use of generative AI tools

units.why: Using AI tools 'to generate content for assignments or exams' is cheating unless the instructor gives 'written authorization', so generated work is barred absent written permission; P19 fits better than P06 because the sentence does not address a silent syllabus.
units.anchor: Using artificial intelligence tools to generate content for assignments or exams
units.frag_start: Using artificial intelligence tools to generate
units.frag_end: without written authorization from the instructor
units.policy: Using artificial intelligence tools, including language models or code generators, to generate content for assignments or exams without written authorization from the instructor is cheating.

units.why: The cheating list bars 'unauthorized use during an examination of ... electronic devices' to 'generate' information; AI is not named but generating information on a device covers it, and the rule is about exams, so P22.
units.anchor: Unauthorized use during an examination of notes, prepared answers, or any electronic devices
units.policy: Unauthorized use during an examination of notes, prepared answers, or any electronic devices such as cell phones, computers, smart watches, or other technologies to copy, retrieve, generate or send information is cheating.

units.why: Submitting 'content generated by ... an AI tool ... as solely your own work' is listed as cheating, so students may present only their own work as their own; this is ownership of submissions (P29), distinct from the citation rule coded separately.
units.anchor: Submitting content generated by another person or an AI tool
units.policy: Submitting content generated by an AI tool as solely your own work is cheating.

units.why: The same sentence calls content 'generated or altered by AI or digital paraphrasing tools without proper citation' cheating, which implies such content is acceptable when cited; this is a citation duty (P24).
units.anchor: content generated or altered by AI or digital paraphrasing tools without proper citation
units.policy: Submitting content generated or altered by AI or digital paraphrasing tools without proper citation is cheating.

units.why: Under plagiarism, 'Copying ... an AI tool's actual words or images without the use of quotation marks and citations' is an example, so AI text must be quoted and cited like any source; P24 is the citation duty.
units.anchor: an AI tool's actual words or images without the use of quotation marks
units.frag_end: attributing the words to their source
units.policy: Copying an AI tool's actual words or images without quotation marks and citations attributing the words to their source is plagiarism.

units.why: 'Unauthorized use of AI-generated content' is listed as plagiarism, so unauthorized AI content is treated as misconduct (P36) under the plagiarism heading.
units.anchor: Unauthorized use of AI-generated content
units.frag_end: citing the AI as the source
units.policy: Unauthorized use of AI-generated content is plagiarism.

units.why: The same sentence makes use of AI-generated content 'even when paraphrased, without citing the AI as the source' plagiarism, a separate rule that paraphrasing does not remove the duty to cite; P24.
units.anchor: even when paraphrased, without citing the AI as the source
units.frag_end: citing the AI as the source
units.policy: Use of AI-generated content, whether in whole or in part, even when paraphrased, without citing the AI as the source is plagiarism.

units.why: The policy states penalties for academic dishonesty, which covers AI misuse through the definitions; 'failing or otherwise reduced grades' and 'suspension or expulsion' are concrete penalties stated in advance (P37).
units.anchor: Penalties for academic dishonesty include academic sanctions, such as failing or otherwise reduced grades

units.why: Listing 'generating entire assignments or exam responses using AI without authorization' as a substantial violation sets the threshold for disciplinary sanctions; it is a penalty-tier rule (P37).
units.anchor: generating entire assignments or exam responses using AI without authorization
units.frag_start: Examples of substantial violations include but
units.policy: Generating entire assignments or exam responses using AI without authorization is an example of a substantial violation, for which the Academic Integrity Officer should seek disciplinary sanctions.

units.why: A reduced grade 'may be an F' set by the faculty member states a concrete academic penalty available to instructors for violations including AI misuse; P37.
units.anchor: A reduced grade may be an "F" or another grade that is lower
units.frag_start: The reduced grade may apply to the
units.frag_end: would have earned but for the violation
units.policy: A reduced grade may be an F or another grade lower than the grade the student would have earned but for the violation, applied to the assignment or the course grade at the faculty member's discretion.

units.why: The policy requires each college to 'subscribe to an electronic plagiarism detection service', a similarity-checking tool; AI is not named, but it is the type for plagiarism software used to identify misuse (P40).
units.anchor: Each college shall subscribe to an electronic plagiarism detection service
units.frag_start: Each college shall subscribe to an
units.frag_end: available for use by the faculty

units.why: 'faculty should inform students of their use' tells instructors to tell students when detection services are used; it is about detection tools (P40), not instructor AI use (P47).
units.anchor: faculty should inform students of their use
units.policy: Faculty should inform students of the use of electronic plagiarism detection services.

units.why: 'shall review with the student the facts and circumstances of the suspected violation whenever feasible' asks instructors to talk with the student before reporting, which is P57.
units.anchor: shall review with the student the facts and circumstances of the suspected violation whenever feasible

units.why: The faculty member 'shall report such incident on a Faculty Report Form' to the Academic Integrity Officer, routing violations (including AI misuse) into the integrity process (P36).
units.anchor: shall report such incident on a Faculty Report Form
units.policy: A faculty member who concludes there has been an incident of academic dishonesty sufficient to affect the student's final course grade reports it on a Faculty Report Form submitted to the college's Academic Integrity Officer, copying the Department Chair.

units.why: The procedure for a student who denies the charge guarantees 'written notice of the charges' and 'the right to appear before the Committee', a right to respond to allegations (P64).
units.anchor: written notice of the charges against them; (ii) the right to appear before the Committee
units.frag_start: These procedures, at a minimum, shall
units.policy: Procedures for hearing cases in which a student denies academic dishonesty provide students at a minimum with written notice of the charges, the right to appear before the Committee, and the right to present witness statements and/or to call witnesses.

units.why: A student who admits dishonesty but contests the sanction 'may appeal the academic sanction through the college's grade appeal process', another route to respond to the outcome of an allegation (P64).
units.anchor: the student may appeal the academic sanction through the college's grade appeal process
units.frag_start: In a case where a student admits

units.why: The explanation says the revision is needed because 'the current policy does not address the advent of Artificial Intelligence'; it states the purpose of the AI revision, an institution-level framework statement (P56).
units.anchor: the current policy does not address the advent of Artificial Intelligence
units.frag_end: its use by students at CUNY

units.why: The explanation says 'Preparing students to learn from and use AI responsibly and ethically is critical' to the mission, a rationale that AI use belongs to the university's purpose; P44 fits better than P56 because it speaks to student preparation.
units.anchor: Preparing students to learn from and use AI responsibly and ethically is critical

units.why: 'students must become facile with the use of AI to learn effectively' and prepare 'for their AI-assisted careers' gives a career-readiness rationale for learning AI use (P44).
units.anchor: students must become facile with the use of AI to learn effectively in today's world
units.frag_end: careers and lives in the future

units.why: 'Each college shall implement this Policy and may adopt its own more specific procedures' sets who maintains and extends the policy; it is an institution-wide framework provision (P56). AI is not named.
units.anchor: may adopt its own more specific procedures to implement the Policy
units.frag_start: Each college shall implement this Policy
units.frag_end: consistent with the policy and procedures described in the Policy
units.policy: Each college shall implement the Policy and may adopt its own more specific procedures, which must be consistent with the Policy.

documents.title: AI and Academic Integrity (LibGuide)
documents.summary: A Hunter Libraries guide page on AI and academic integrity. It warns about unreliable AI citations, recommends transparency, quotes the AI parts of the CUNY policy, and reproduces Chicago Manual of Style guidance on citing chatbot content.
documents.stance_why: The guide sets no rule of its own; it recommends transparency, quotes the CUNY policy that AI use must follow 'the usage policy for specific assignments', and gives citation guidance, so the decision on use stays with instructors and assignments.

units.why: The guide warns of 'inconsistency across all varieties of AI tools in providing context and citation', which tells students AI output cannot be trusted to be sourced; P31 (verify AI output).

units.anchor: we also cannot be confident in declaring that no AI tool does

units.why: The guide names 'Citing AI tools and AI generated information' as a main academic-integrity concern; it frames a citation duty without stating a rule, so P24 with informs.
units.anchor: Citing AI tools and AI generated information

units.why: 'our recommendation is to be as transparent as possible when using an AI tool for your research' recommends disclosure of AI use; the library recommends, so modality should, P24.
units.anchor: be as transparent as possible when using an AI tool for your research

units.why: 'we do not recommend using an AI tool for your research' when sources cannot be properly cited discourages AI use without banning it, which is P03.

units.policy: If you cannot guarantee that the information included in your research can be properly cited and sourced, the library does not recommend using an AI tool for your research.

units.why: 'AI is not responsible for your academic integrity' puts responsibility on the student, so P29 (students own what they submit).

notes: No school-level or computing-unit AI policy found at Hunter; coded layers are the CUNY system policy, Hunter's posting of it, and the library guide. The Hunter page and library guide repeat the CUNY text, so shared units are coded again in each document, as instructed. Skipped as not AI-related: posting the policy in the LMS, orientation, file retention, uploading work to homework aggregators, falsification of records. The plagiarism-detection and exam-device units are included although AI is not named.
